Introduction to Personal Finance Personal finance is the practice of managing your money, including budgeting, saving, investing, borrowing, and planning for future needs such as retirement or large purchases.

Good personal-finance habits generally rest on four pillars: spending less than you earn, maintaining an emergency fund, avoiding high-interest debt, and saving consistently for long-term goals. Financial advisors commonly recommend reviewing your finances at least once per quarter, and creating a full household budget at least once per year. 2.

Building an Emergency Fund An emergency fund is a cash reserve set aside to cover unexpected expenses, such as medical bills, car repairs, or a sudden loss of income. Most financial planners recommend saving enough to cover 3 to 6 months of essential living expenses. Freelancers, contractors, or single-income households are often advised to aim for the higher end of this range, sometimes up to 9 months of expenses, because their income is less predictable.

Where to keep it: ● A high-yield savings account, which as of this guide typically earns between 4% and 5% annual interest. ● A separate account from everyday checking, to reduce the temptation to spend it. ● Funds should remain liquid and low-risk — not invested in stocks. 3.

Budgeting: The 50/30/20 Rule The 50/30/20 rule is a simple budgeting framework for dividing after-tax (take-home) income into three categories: Category Share of Income Examples Needs 50% Rent/mortgage, groceries, utilities, insurance, minimum debt payments Wants 30% Dining out, entertainment, subscriptions, travel Savings & Debt Payoff 20% Emergency fund, retirement contributions, extra debt payments Example: on a take-home income of $4,000 per month, this rule suggests roughly $2,000 for needs, $1,200 for wants, and $800 for savings and debt payoff.

4. Saving for Retirement Retirement accounts offer tax advantages to encourage long-term saving. Two common U.S. account types referenced in this guide are the 401(k) and the Individual Retirement Account (IRA). ● A common rule of thumb is to save at least 15% of pre-tax income for retirement each year, including any employer match. ● Many employers match 401(k) contributions up to 4% to 6% of salary — financial advisors generally recommend contributing at least enough to capture the full match.

● A widely cited guideline suggests having the equivalent of your annual salary saved by age 30, three times your salary by age 40, and six times your salary by age 50. 5. Understanding Credit Scores A credit score is a numerical rating, typically ranging from 300 to 850, that estimates how likely a person is to repay borrowed money. The most widely used scoring model is the FICO score.

Score Range Rating 800 - 850 Exceptional 740 - 799 Very Good 670 - 739 Good 580 - 669 Fair 300 - 579 Poor A score of 670 or above is generally considered the threshold for qualifying for favorable interest rates on loans and credit cards. The five main factors affecting a FICO score are: payment history (35%), amounts owed (30%), length of credit history (15%), new credit (10%), and credit mix (10%). 6.

Debt Management Strategies Two popular strategies for paying off multiple debts are the debt snowball method and the debt avalanche method. Debt Snowball Pay off debts from smallest balance to largest, regardless of interest rate, while making minimum payments on the rest. This method prioritizes psychological momentum from quick wins. Debt Avalanche Pay off debts from highest interest rate to lowest, regardless of balance.

This method minimizes the total interest paid over time and is generally the mathematically optimal approach. As a general guideline, a household's total monthly debt payments (excluding mortgage) should not exceed 20% of take-home pay, and total debt-to-income ratio including a mortgage should generally stay below 36%. 7.
